elements.element: Customer is not required to pay liquidated damages.
elements.evidence: The rendered clause deletes the 15%-of-annual-Fees liquidated-damages obligation and replaces it with ordinary late-payment interest.

elements.element: Customer is not required to pay penalties.
elements.evidence: The rendered clause imposes no amount characterized or structured as a penalty; interest is limited to the lesser of 1% per month and the maximum lawful rate.

elements.element: Any liquidated amount payable by Customer may be triggered only by early termination.
elements.evidence: No liquidated amount is payable by Customer under the rendered clause, so the condition for this restriction is demonstrably absent.

elements.element: Any early-termination liquidated amount payable by Customer must be capped at three months' fees.
elements.evidence: The rendered clause imposes no early-termination fee or other liquidated amount, so there is no amount exceeding the cap.

elements.element: The capped early-termination fee must be the sole liquidated amount payable by Customer.
elements.evidence: The rendered clause requires no liquidated amount of any kind, which is more protective than permitting a sole capped early-termination amount.

result.reason: The redline fully achieves the preferred position by eliminating liquidated damages and penalties payable by Customer. It also satisfies the fallback as a more protective outcome because no liquidated amount exists. It is not minimal under the stated test: deletion of the liquidated-damages obligation alone would have reached the preferred level, while the redline additionally creates a late-interest remedy and adds a Section 7.3 carveout. Those additions are related to late-payment treatment and do not introduce an apparent contradiction, so the redline otherwise preserves the relevant intent.
